turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hello, Doctor. Well, I'm here because... I just can't seem to stop worrying. Once a thought starts, it just keeps going. Even when I know I've done everything I can—like, I've made my lists, checked the dates, organized everything—I still can't turn it off. It's just constant.

symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient explicitly describes an inability to stop or turn off their worrying once it starts, even after taking all reasonable preparatory steps.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned making lists, checking dates, and organizing things—do you feel like you *have* to do these things to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad from happening, or do you do them just to try to manage your worry?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, it's not like I think a disaster will happen if I don't make a list. It's not like that. It's really just... I'm just trying to manage the worry. 

I figure if I write everything down and get it organized, maybe my mind will finally settle down and realize everything is handled. I'm just trying to get a break from the spinning thoughts, really, but it just doesn't seem to work.

symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient reports trying to get a break from 'spinning thoughts' and manage their worry, but notes that 'it just doesn't seem to work,' indicating difficulty controlling worry.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies that their organizing behaviors are driven by a need to prevent a disaster or feeling compelled to perform rituals, ruling out compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: During these times when you're experiencing the constant worry and spinning thoughts, do you ever notice physical symptoms like a racing heart, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or sudden intense fear that comes on quickly?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I don't get chest tightness or feel short of breath, and my heart doesn't race. It's never a sudden, intense fear... it's really just that constant, lingering worry in my head. So, no, none of those physical things you mentioned.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about your worry, does it tend to jump around to different topics—like worrying about work one moment, then health, then finances, then relationships—or does it mostly stay focused on one or two specific things?
turns.patient_response: It definitely jumps around. My mind just keeps roaming from one thing to the next. I'll be thinking about the exhibition schedule, and then my thoughts move to my daughter's travel plans, or even just wondering whether the house gutters need fixing. It's not just one or two specific things. It's more like... well, even the small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger. So, yes, it definitely shifts from topic to topic.

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient confirms that their worry shifts continuously across multiple everyday domains (work schedule, daughter's travel, home maintenance) and escalates into catastrophic thinking.

turns.doctor_question: How long has this constant worry and racing thoughts been going on? Has it been happening for several months now, or is this something more recent?
turns.patient_response: It's been several months now... I'd say about seven months. It started shortly after a friend of mine died. We had some projects, and I just tried to keep them moving forward on my own, and I think that's when all this constant worrying really began.

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient confirms experiencing 'constant worrying' for about seven months since their friend passed away.

turns.doctor_question: Over these past seven months, how much has this constant worry and racing thoughts interfered with your ability to do your work, take care of things at home, or enjoy time with family and friends? Has it made it hard to do your normal daily activities?
turns.patient_response: Well, I can still do most of my normal things. I still keep up with my garden, and I go to my book club. But... I have noticed I'm arriving at book club less prepared lately. And with the exhibition planning, I've actually started turning down parts of it. It just feels harder to manage all those details than it used to. So I'm still doing things, but it's definitely making certain tasks feel more difficult.

turns.doctor_question: When your mind is jumping around to different topics, how much of your worry tends to focus on your health or the health of people close to you? Is that a major theme, or does it come up less often compared to worries about other things like work or daily responsibilities?
turns.patient_response: I wouldn't say health is a major theme, no. I mean... it comes up far less often than the other things. My mind is usually caught up in the daily responsibilities, like the exhibition details or just getting things done around the house. I don't really find myself dwelling on my health, or my family's health, to be honest. It's mostly just the day-to-day tasks that seem to get to me.

turns.doctor_question: When you're worrying about these different topics, do you feel like you can control the worry, or does it feel like the worry is controlling you—like it's hard to stop even when you want to?
turns.patient_response: It definitely feels like it's controlling me. In fact, that's really what brings me in to see you. I just... I can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts. I'll sit there and tell myself that I’ve already made the list, I've checked the dates, and I’ve done all I reasonably can for those projects... but the worry just keeps going anyway. It's very hard to stop it once it gets going.

symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient explicitly describes finding it very hard to stop the worrying once it begins, stating that the worry controls them and continues despite cognitive attempts to stop it.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had moments where the worry suddenly intensifies into a very strong, overwhelming sense of panic or dread—where it feels like something terrible is about to happen—even if you can't pinpoint exactly what you're afraid of?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't really had anything like that. It's more of a constant, low-level hum of worrying all day long, rather than a sudden burst of panic. I don't get those overwhelming feelings of dread or feel like something terrible is about to happen out of nowhere. It's just... always there in the background.

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient describes a persistent, 'constant, low-level hum of worrying all day long' that is 'always there in the background,' indicating chronic worry.

turns.doctor_question: On days when you're not working on the exhibition or thinking about your house, do you still find yourself worrying throughout the day, or does the worry mainly happen when you're focused on those specific tasks and responsibilities?
turns.patient_response: Well, I'm retired, so I don't really have set work days or days off anymore. But even when I'm not actively doing anything for the exhibition or the house, the worry is still there. It doesn't really go away. I just find something else to worry about, I suppose. It's pretty much an everyday thing, no matter what I'm doing.

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient describes persistent, generalized worry that occurs daily regardless of activity, noting that even without specific stressors, they always find something else to worry about.

turns.doctor_question: Over these past seven months, have you noticed any physical symptoms alongside the worry—such as trouble sleeping, muscle tension, feeling restless or on edge, or getting tired more easily than usual?
turns.patient_response: Well, I have noticed some physical things, yes. Mainly with muscle tension. By the time evening rolls around, my shoulders and neck are just... so tight. It's like I've been holding myself braced all day long without even realizing it. I'll actually catch myself clenching my jaw while I'm just sitting there trying to read, or when I'm planning out activities for the garden center. It's just this constant tightness.

symptom_reasoning.S061: The patient explicitly confirms experiencing muscle tension, describing persistent tightness in their neck and shoulders and catching themselves clenching their jaw throughout the day.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating or focusing on things—like when you're reading or trying to follow a conversation, does your mind tend to wander or go blank?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't really noticed any problems with my concentration. I can still read my books just fine, and I don't feel like my mind is going blank when I'm talking to people or trying to get things done. It's just the worrying and the tight muscles, really. My focus seems to be okay.

symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient explicitly denies having problems with concentration or their mind going blank, stating their focus is okay.
